Epilogue

EP-ih-log -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, EP. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Epilogue is a concluding section at the end of a book or play.

Don't skip the epilogue -- it reveals who finally ended up keeping the dog.

Worked Example

The mystery wraps up on page 300: culprit caught, jewels returned. Then comes one last chapter, set a full year later -- the inspector, retired now and tending her garden, opens her mailbox to find a postcard with no signature, only a drawing of a jewel. She smiles.

That final year-later chapter is the epilogue: a concluding section that comes AFTER the main story has already ended, giving readers one last glimpse -- what became of everyone, and sometimes one final tease. Epilogues often announce themselves with a time jump: 'ten years later...'

How Epilogue Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

afterword

afterword: a closing section after the main text

conclusion

conclusion: the final, wrapping-up part

coda

coda: a finishing passage that rounds a work off

Antonyms

prologue

prologue: an opening section before the story begins

preface

preface: an author's introductory note

How Strong Is It? — conclusion → epilogue → coda

conclusion vs. epilogue

conclusion vs. epilogue: Conclusion is the plainest word -- every essay and story has one, simply because everything ends.

coda vs. epilogue

coda vs. epilogue: Coda is the strongest and most artful: borrowed from music, it names a deliberately crafted tailpiece added after the ending proper -- exactly the flourish a well-written epilogue provides.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of epilogue.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — epi-

prefix — epi-: upon, in addition (Greek)

root — logue

root — logue: word, speech (Greek logos)

Put it together

Put it together: Epilogue is Greek for 'words added on' -- epi- ('upon, in addition') plus logos ('word, speech'). In ancient theater, the epilogos was the speech delivered after the play was over, when an actor stepped forward to add a few final words. The word still means exactly that: the extra words laid on top of a finished story.

Use the root in a new word: epicenter

Use the root in a new word: epicenter: News crews gathered at the epicenter of the earthquake.

Root Check

Word Choice

Epilogue and prologue are bookends: the prologue speaks before the story, the epilogue after it. An epilogue usually continues the STORY itself -- often after a time jump -- showing what became of the characters; an afterword, by contrast, is typically the author stepping out of the story to speak as themselves. If the characters are still on stage, it is an epilogue.
